title: The Seventy-Two, the Good Samaritan, and Mary's Choice
summary: Jesus sends seventy-two disciples (seventy in many manuscripts) ahead of him in pairs to heal and to announce that the kingdom of God has come near, pronounces woes on the unrepentant towns of Galilee, and rejoices when the messengers return. An expert in the law asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus answers his follow-up question, “And who is my neighbor?”, with the parable of the Good Samaritan. In a village Martha busily serves while her sister Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the good portion.
story:
Jesus has just set his face toward Jerusalem (9:51), a Samaritan village has refused him, and James and John have wanted to call down fire on it (9:52-56). Three would-be followers have been told what following costs (9:57-62). Now the mission widens. In chapter 9 the Twelve were sent to the towns of Galilee; here a larger company is sent ahead of Jesus along the road he is about to travel, to prepare his way as John the Baptist once did. Their success draws from Jesus a burst of joyful prayer to the Father, one of the rare places in Luke where we overhear the Son speaking about his own relation to the Father.

Then Luke sets side by side two scenes found only in his Gospel, which together answer the question the lawyer asks about eternal life. The Samaritan shows what it means to love one's neighbor, and Mary shows what it means to love God by listening to the Lord's word. The Samaritan hero lands with special force a few verses after a Samaritan village turned Jesus away and the disciples wanted it burned. The chapter moves from mission to prayer to love, and it closes in a house, with a woman at the feet of the one who has been teaching all along.
historical:
The number of the messengers is uncertain in the manuscripts. Seventy-two is read in verses 1 and 17 by P75 (the Bodmer papyrus of Luke and John, around AD 175 to 225), Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and early Latin and Syriac translations; seventy is read by Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Ephraemi, and the mass of later manuscripts. Bruce Metzger judged the evidence almost evenly balanced (New Testament Studies 5, 1959), and the editors of the standard Greek text print the word two in brackets. Zachary Cole (New Testament Studies 63, 2017) showed that P45, the Chester Beatty papyrus, had been misreported at verse 17 and actually supports seventy-two, and argued that scribes more often dropped a digit from a compound number than added one. Both numbers carry meaning. Genesis 10 lists the descendants of Noah's sons, the nations of the world, as seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek Septuagint, so either number can point to a mission that reaches all peoples. Moses gathered seventy elders to share his burden, and Eldad and Medad, who were among those registered but stayed in the camp, prophesied as well (Numbers 11:16-29), a scene some readers see behind these extra workers. The Letter of Aristeas says seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, translated the Law into Greek, and Sidney Jellicoe (1960) argued Luke had that story in view. Eusebius (Church History 1.12) says no list of the seventy survives, though tradition counted Barnabas, Sosthenes, Matthias, and Thaddaeus among them; the Orthodox Church keeps the Synaxis of the Seventy Apostles on 4 January.

The towns Jesus names lay close together at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Chorazin, about two and a half miles north of Capernaum in the basalt hills, is mentioned only here and in Matthew 11:21; the visible ruins, including a synagogue with a carved basalt seat inscribed in Aramaic and now in the Israel Museum, date from the third or fourth century, after the town Jesus knew. Bethsaida, the home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip (John 1:44), is disputed between et-Tell, excavated by Rami Arav from 1987, and el-Araj on the lakeshore, excavated since 2016 by Mordechai Aviam and R. Steven Notley, where a Byzantine church has been found that its excavators identify with the Church of the Apostles seen by the pilgrim Willibald in the eighth century. Tyre and Sidon, the old Phoenician ports, stood under the prophets' oracles (Isaiah 23, Ezekiel 26 to 28).

The road from Jerusalem to Jericho, which Josephus puts at 150 stadia, about seventeen miles (Jewish War 4.474), drops some 3,300 feet from Jerusalem's ridge to Jericho, which lies about 850 feet below sea level. It crosses the Judean wilderness by a pass Joshua 15:7 calls the Ascent of Adummim, the red ascent, from the color of its rock. Jerome, recounting Paula's pilgrimage (Letter 108), explained the name as blood shed there by robbers and connected the place with this parable, and pilgrims were later shown an inn on the road; a Byzantine hostel has been excavated at Khan al-Hatrura, which since 2009 has housed a museum of mosaics. The Babylonian Talmud (Taanit 27a) preserves a tradition that half of each priestly course lived in Jericho, so priests and Levites commuting to their weeks of temple service used this road.

The hostility between Jews and Samaritans was centuries deep and recently inflamed. John Hyrcanus had destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254-256), around 110 BC by the evidence of the coins. Under the governor Coponius (AD 6 to 9), Samaritans scattered human bones in the temple porticoes at Passover (Antiquities 18.29-30), and around AD 52 Samaritan villagers killed Galilean pilgrims at Ginae, setting off reprisals (Antiquities 20.118-136). A saying attributed to Rabbi Eliezer compared eating Samaritan bread to eating pork (m. Sheviit 8:10).
cultural:
The instructions to the messengers assume village hospitality. A household that received a traveler took on his care, and the guest in turn was expected not to shop around for better lodging (verse 7). The greeting of peace, shalom, was a blessing and not merely a hello. A son of peace (the literal Greek behind man of peace in verse 6) is a Semitic idiom for a person marked by and open to that peace. Not greeting anyone on the road recalls Elisha's order to Gehazi (2 Kings 4:29): greetings in the East could be long and ceremonial, and the errand was urgent. Eating whatever is set before them (verses 7 and 8) would matter once the mission reached homes where purity rules were kept differently, a concern Luke returns to in Acts 10. Shaking off the dust of a town was a public sign of breaking fellowship and leaving the town to answer for itself (9:5, Acts 13:51).

The lawyer (nomikos) was an expert in the Law of Moses, what Luke elsewhere calls a scribe. His answer joins the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:5, which devout Jews recited morning and evening (m. Berakhot 1:1-4), with Leviticus 19:18. Jewish teachers also sought the Torah's great principle: Rabbi Akiva named love of neighbor, and his colleague Ben Azzai named Genesis 5:1, the creation of every human being in God's likeness (Sifra, Kedoshim). Leviticus 19:18 speaks of loving your neighbor in the setting of your own people, and 19:34 extends the same love to the foreigner living among Israel. The lawyer's question presses on that boundary.

In the parable, a priest who touched a corpse became unclean (Leviticus 21:1-3), and a man left half dead might be taken for dead. Yet the Mishnah requires even the high priest and a Nazirite to defile themselves to bury an abandoned corpse, a met mitzvah (m. Nazir 7:1), and both men are going down from Jerusalem, away from their service. Jesus gives them no reason. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) points out that a Jewish hearer, after a priest and a Levite, would expect the third figure to be an ordinary Israelite; the shock is that the rescuer is the enemy. The victim is stripped and unconscious, so no one could tell his people by his clothing or his speech. Oil soothed and wine cleansed wounds (compare Isaiah 1:6). Remarkably, 2 Chronicles 28:15 tells how men of the northern kingdom, whose capital was Samaria, clothed captives from Judah, anointed them, put the feeble on donkeys, and brought them to Jericho. The inn (pandocheion, a lodging that takes in all comers) had a poor reputation, and the Samaritan, a foreigner in Judea, leaves an open account in his own name. A denarius was a day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2); Polybius (Histories 2.15) notes that inns in northern Italy rarely charged more than half an as a day, a small fraction of a denarius, so two denarii bought real time, though prices varied widely.

Sitting at someone's feet was the posture of a disciple; Paul says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). For a woman to take that place in a mixed household, rather than joining the work of hospitality that fell to women, crossed a line of expectation. Martha is named as the one who received Jesus, and many manuscripts add into her house, which makes her the householder.
literary:
The chapter has three movements. The mission of the seventy-two (1-24) mirrors the sending of the Twelve in 9:1-6 and anticipates the church's mission in Acts; it runs from sending to warning to return and ends in prayer and blessing. The dialogue with the lawyer (25-37) is built in two matching rounds, each with a question from the lawyer, a counter-question from Jesus, the lawyer's answer, and a command to act: “Do this and you will live” and “Go and do likewise.” The parable sits between the rounds and turns the lawyer's question inside out. He asked whom he must count as a neighbor, looking for the edge of the obligation; Jesus asks which of the three became a neighbor, and the only possible answer is the one the lawyer will not name, so he says the one who showed him mercy.

The parable is told with triple rhythm. The priest saw him and passed by on the other side; the Levite saw him and passed by on the other side; the Samaritan saw him and had compassion. The same verb of seeing leads to opposite actions, and the Samaritan's compassion then unfolds in a rush of verbs: he went to him, bandaged, poured, set him on his animal, brought him, cared for him, paid, and promised to return. The scene of Martha and Mary (38-42) follows at once, so that active love for the neighbor and attentive love for the Lord are set side by side as the two halves of the great commandment. Luke often pairs a man and a woman in this way. Where Mark and Matthew place the question about the great commandment in Jerusalem in the last week (Mark 12:28-34, Matthew 22:34-40), Luke has it here and omits it later, and the same question about inheriting eternal life returns on the lips of a rich ruler in 18:18. Verses 21 and 22 have a close parallel in Matthew 11:25-27, and their language of the Father and the Son knowing one another sounds so much like John's Gospel that Karl von Hase (Geschichte Jesu, 1876) called it a meteor from the Johannine sky. The repeated name, “Martha, Martha”, is a mark of tender urgency, as with Simon in 22:31.

outline.t: Jesus rejoices in the Father's revelation
The lawyer's question: love God and neighbor
The parable of the Good Samaritan

doctrines.note: The harvest is plentiful and the workers few, so the disciples first pray to the Lord of the harvest and then go as the answer to their own prayer (verse 2). They go in pairs, vulnerable as lambs among wolves, dependent on hospitality, carrying peace, healing, and the news that God's kingdom has come near. Whoever hears them hears Jesus, and whoever rejects them rejects the Father who sent him (verse 16).

In verses 21 and 22 Jesus rejoices in the Holy Spirit, praises the Father as Lord of heaven and earth, and claims a knowledge shared only by the Father and the Son. All things have been entrusted to the Son, and the Father is known only by those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. It is one of the clearest glimpses in the first three Gospels of the relation of Father, Son, and Spirit.

The Father hides these things from the wise and learned and reveals them to little children (verse 21), and he does it through the Son (verse 22). Knowledge of God here is not an achievement of intellect but a gift received by the humble, and the disciples are blessed to see what prophets and kings longed to see (verses 23 and 24).

The Law's heart is love for God with the whole self and love for the neighbor as oneself (verse 27). The parable refuses to let that love be fenced: the neighbor is whoever lies wounded in my path, and love is shown in mercy that costs time, risk, and money. Mary's listening shows the other half, love for God as attentive devotion to the Lord's word.

Jesus sends the lawyer back to the Law itself (verse 26) and affirms his summary of it. The command “Do this and you will live” echoes Leviticus 18:5. Jesus does not lower the Law's demand; he shows how far it reaches, and in the rest of Luke eternal life comes to those who receive him and his mercy (7:50, 19:9-10), of which such love is the fruit.

words.note: Therismos, harvest. It occurs 13 times in the New Testament, three of them in this verse. In the prophets harvest is an image of God's final gathering and judgment (Joel 3:13, Isaiah 27:12), and Jesus uses it for the present moment of mission: the time of gathering has already begun. God is the Lord of the harvest, and the workers are sent into his field, not their own.

Eirēnē, peace. It occurs about 91 times in the New Testament, 14 of them in Luke, more than in any other Gospel. It usually renders the Hebrew shalom, the wholeness and well-being God gives, not merely the absence of conflict. The angels announce peace on earth (2:14), and here the messengers speak peace to a house; if no son of peace is there, the peace returns to them, as though the blessing were something with a life of its own.

Klēronomeō, to inherit, to receive as a possession. It occurs 18 times in the New Testament. In the Old Testament Israel inherits the land as God's gift, and later Jewish usage speaks of inheriting the world to come. The lawyer's question, what must I do to inherit, already contains a tension, since an inheritance is not earned but received by a child; the same question returns in 18:18.

Plēsion, neighbor, literally the one near. It occurs 17 times in the New Testament, usually in quotations of Leviticus 19:18, where the Hebrew rea' means a fellow member of the covenant people. Standard lexicons note that Greek usage could mean simply the person nearby. The lawyer wants a definition that marks where obligation stops; Jesus turns the noun into an action, asking who became a neighbor.

Splagchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from splagchna, the inward parts thought of as the seat of feeling. It occurs 12 times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels, and almost always of Jesus or of a figure in his parables who acts as God acts. Luke uses it three times: of Jesus at the widow's funeral at Nain (7:13), of the Samaritan (10:33), and of the father who runs to his returning son (15:20).

Eleos, mercy. It occurs about 27 times in the New Testament, six of them in Luke. In the Septuagint it usually renders hesed, God's loyal covenant love, and the lawyer's phrase in verse 37, literally the one who did mercy with him, echoes the Hebrew idiom for showing hesed. He cannot bring himself to say the Samaritan, but his answer names exactly what the Law was about (Hosea 6:6).

Diakonia, service, ministry. It occurs 34 times in the New Testament, only here in the Gospels, and eight times in Acts, where it names the apostles' ministry of the word (Acts 6:4) and the daily distribution of food (6:1). Martha is distracted by much diakonia, and the verb diakoneō follows in verse 40. The word's later use for church ministry lies behind modern debates over whether the scene commends or restricts women's service.

Meris, part, share, portion. It occurs five times in the New Testament. In the Septuagint it is the word for the Levites' portion, where God himself is their share instead of land (Numbers 18:20), and for the psalmists' confession that the Lord is their portion (Psalm 16:5, 73:26). Mary has chosen the good portion, and unlike a portion of food or land, it will not be taken from her.

christ:
Jesus sends messengers ahead of his face, the language Luke uses of John the Baptist as the messenger of Malachi 3:1 (7:27), and he says that to hear them is to hear him and to reject them is to reject the Father who sent him. He sees Satan fall like lightning from heaven, an image drawn from Isaiah 14:12-15, where the king of Babylon who would climb to heaven is cast down; the woe on Capernaum in verse 15 uses the same passage. The authority to trample snakes and scorpions recalls both the serpent of Genesis 3:15 and the promise of Psalm 91:13. The chapter thus presents the ministry of Jesus and his messengers as the beginning of the defeat of the powers that hold humanity captive, which Luke will show complete in the cross, resurrection, and ascension.

In verses 21 and 22 Jesus speaks as the Son who alone knows the Father and who reveals him to whom he wills. This is the Christology the church later confessed in the creeds, found here in tradition shared by Matthew and Luke, not only in John. The prophets and kings who longed to see what the disciples see (verse 24) wanted to see the day of the Messiah.

From the second century, many interpreters read the Good Samaritan as a picture of Christ himself, who comes to wounded humanity when the Law and the prophets pass by. In context the parable answers a question about how to love one's neighbor, and it should be taught first that way. Yet the link is not arbitrary. The compassion the Samaritan shows is the very word Luke uses of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the father in the parable of the lost son (15:20), and Jesus himself was the rejected outsider whom a Samaritan village refused and whom his own leaders would reject. The one who tells the story embodies it: he crosses every boundary, binds wounds, pays the cost, and promises to return. Mary's choice points the same way. The one thing needed is to sit at the Lord's feet and hear his word, for the Lord in this house is the one in whom the Father is revealed.
interpretation:
The allegorical reading of the Good Samaritan is ancient. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.17.3, around 180) saw the Lord commending humanity to the Holy Spirit and the two denarii as the image of the Father and the Son. Clement of Alexandria (Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? 28-29) asked who the neighbor could be but the Savior himself. Origen (Homilies on Luke 34) reported an elder's reading in which the wounded man is Adam, Jerusalem paradise, Jericho the world, the robbers hostile powers, the priest the Law, the Levite the prophets, the Samaritan Christ, the animal his body, the inn the church, and the two denarii the Father and the Son. Augustine (Questions on the Gospels 2.19) made Jericho mortality, the inn the church, the innkeeper the apostle Paul, and the denarii the two commandments of love. Ambrose (Exposition of Luke 7.73-84, about 387) read the Samaritan as the Son of Man come down from heaven, and Jerome placed the parable at the Ascent of Adummim. This reading ruled the Middle Ages, and the thirteenth-century Good Samaritan window at Chartres (about 1205 to 1215) sets the parable beside the creation and fall of Adam. The sixth-century Rossano Gospels already paints the Samaritan with a cross-marked halo.

The Reformers kept the parable's moral force; Calvin (Harmony of the Gospels, 1555) dismissed the allegory that defenders of free will had drawn from the half-dead man as too far-fetched to need refuting. Adolf Jülicher (Die Gleichnisreden Jesu, 1888 to 1899) made rejection of allegory a principle of modern study, and C. H. Dodd, Joachim Jeremias, and John Dominic Crossan (In Parables, 1973) read the parable as a shock that overturns the hearer's world. Søren Kierkegaard's Works of Love (1847) took the neighbor to be every person, loved because God commands it. Martin Luther King Jr., in his final speech in Memphis on 3 April 1968, retold the Jericho road and turned the priest's question, what will happen to me if I stop, into the Samaritan's question, what will happen to him if I do not. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) has pressed Christians to stop explaining the priest and Levite by Jewish purity law, which the text never mentions, and to hear the story's demand that one see the enemy as a neighbor.

Martha and Mary became the church's classic figures of the active and contemplative lives. John Cassian (Conferences 1.8) and Augustine (Sermons 103 and 104) ranked Mary's contemplation above Martha's service, which belongs to this passing age, and Gregory the Great fixed the pairing for the Middle Ages. Meister Eckhart (German Sermon 86) reversed the ranking and praised Martha as the more mature, and Teresa of Ávila (Interior Castle 7.4, 1577) insisted that Martha and Mary must work together to entertain the Lord. Until 1950 the Roman Missal read verses 38 to 42 at the feast of the Assumption. Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza (1986) and Barbara Reid (Choosing the Better Part?, 1996) argued that the story silences Martha's ministry, while others, such as Ben Witherington III (Women in the Ministry of Jesus, 1984), read it as welcoming women as disciples. Velázquez (1618, National Gallery, London) and Vermeer (about 1655, Scottish National Gallery) painted the scene; Rembrandt, Delacroix (1849), and Van Gogh (1890, after Delacroix) painted the Samaritan. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the chapter over three Sundays in Year C (Propers 9 to 11), and the 1662 Prayer Book appoints verses 23 to 37 for the thirteenth Sunday after Trinity.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verses 1 and 17 the King James Version, the NKJV, and the NASB read seventy, while the ESV, NIV, CSB, NRSV, and BSB read seventy-two; the witnesses are described in the historical note, and each version prints the other number in a footnote. In verse 15 the older Byzantine text, followed by the King James Version, reads a statement, ‘which art exalted unto heaven’, where the earliest manuscripts read a question expecting the answer no, ‘will you be lifted up to heaven?’, which suits the allusion to Isaiah 14. In verse 21 the earliest manuscripts say Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, while later ones, followed by the KJV, say ‘in spirit’.

In verse 38 Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Bezae, and most manuscripts say that Martha received him into her house, while P45, P75, and Codex Vaticanus lack the phrase; Jennifer Wyant (2019) has argued that it is original and was dropped. The largest difference is in verses 41 and 42, which survive in three forms. P45, P75, Codex Alexandrinus, and most later manuscripts read ‘only one thing is necessary’, the text of the BSB and most versions. P3, Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and some Coptic witnesses read ‘few things are needed, or only one’, which Westcott and Hort printed and John Cassian quoted (Conferences 1.8); it softens Jesus' word into a remark about a simple meal before lifting it to the one thing. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts omit the words about worry over many things and the one thing needed, so that Jesus says only that Martha is troubled and that Mary has chosen the good portion. Most editors judge the short ‘one thing’ reading original.

teach.big: The kingdom that has come near in Jesus sends his people out in dependence and joy, and it defines eternal life as love without limits for God and neighbor, received and lived by those who sit at his feet.

outline.t: Mission begins with prayer for workers and goes out in vulnerability, carrying peace, healing, and the announcement that God's kingdom is near.
Great privilege brings great accountability; the towns that saw the most were judged the most strictly, and rejecting the messenger is rejecting the Sender.
Real spiritual power is given, but the disciple's deepest joy is not success in ministry; it is being known and named by God.
The Son reveals the Father to the humble, and those who see Jesus see what prophets and kings longed for.
The Law already names the way of life, love for God and neighbor; the danger is using theology to limit whom we must love.
The question is not who qualifies as my neighbor but whether I will become a neighbor to whoever is wounded in my path, even across the deepest hostility.
Service without listening becomes anxious and resentful; the one thing needed is to receive the Lord's word, a portion no one can take away.

teach.pitfalls:
Preachers often explain the priest and Levite as bound by purity rules, which turns the parable into a lesson about Jewish legalism. The text gives them no reason, they are leaving Jerusalem, and later Jewish law required burying an abandoned body, so the explanation both misreads the story and repeats an old caricature of Judaism. The point is closer to home: religious people with good reasons pass by. A second misreading reduces the Samaritan to general niceness, forgetting that the hero is the hated outsider and that the lawyer is being asked to see an enemy as the model of obedience. A third skips straight to the allegory of Christ as the Samaritan and never lets the command, Go and do likewise, land. The opposite error forbids any Christological echo at all, when Luke's own vocabulary of compassion invites it.

With Martha and Mary, avoid preaching a contest between personality types or between busy and quiet Christians. Martha is not rebuked for serving, which Jesus praises elsewhere (22:26-27), but for anxiety and for asking Jesus to pull Mary away from his word. Avoid also using the scene to confine women to either the kitchen or silence; Luke presents a woman in the disciple's place. With verses 17 to 20, avoid making spiritual power or visible results the measure of faithfulness, and with verse 7, avoid using the worker's wages to justify ministry for gain, which the same passage forbids by sending them without purse or bag.
teach.pastoral: The Good Samaritan will press on people who have been left half dead by others, including those whose religious leaders passed by when they were abused or abandoned. Name that honestly: the parable condemns the passing by, and the one who stops is the one who pleases God. It may also burden conscientious people who feel responsible for every need they see; the Samaritan helps the man in front of him and hands him to an innkeeper, and love does not require one person to carry the whole world. Martha's complaint gives voice to the exhaustion of caregivers and of those, often women, who carry unseen work in homes and churches; Jesus speaks to her by name and gently, not with contempt. The joy of names written in heaven is good news for those whose ministry has seemed to fail.

hard.q: Does “Do this and you will live” teach that eternal life is earned by keeping the law?
hard.a:
The objection is plain. Asked how to inherit eternal life, Jesus points to the Law, approves the lawyer's summary, and says “Do this and you will live”, echoing Leviticus 18:5. He says nothing about faith, grace, forgiveness, or himself. To many critics this is evidence that the historical Jesus taught a Jewish way of Torah obedience and that the later Christian gospel of grace, especially in Paul, departed from him; William Wrede's study of Paul (1904) famously called the apostle the second founder of Christianity. Jewish readers make a related point from the other side: the passage agrees with Judaism, in which the Torah is itself God's gracious gift and the way of life for his covenant people, a pattern E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) called covenantal nomism. On this reading, Christian embarrassment at verse 28 says more about Christian theology than about Jesus.

Christian interpreters answer in several ways. Calvin (Harmony of the Gospels, 1555) argued that Christ accommodated his reply to the lawyer's question: the Law truly describes perfect righteousness, and no one is justified by it only because no one keeps it, so the command exposes the lawyer's need, which his wish to justify himself (verse 29) confirms. Many Lutheran and Reformed preachers read the passage this way, as the Law doing its work of showing sin. Augustine (On the Spirit and the Letter, 412) and the Catholic and Orthodox traditions, with many recent Protestant scholars, stress instead that Jesus means what he says: those who inherit life are those who love, and such love is itself the gift of grace working through faith, so the command is not a trap but a description of the life God gives. Others note that in Luke's larger story eternal life comes to those who receive Jesus (7:50, 18:18-30, 19:9-10) and that the same Gospel ends with forgiveness preached in his name (24:47). These readings differ in emphasis more than in substance, and all agree that Jesus does not lower the command or treat love as optional.

hard.q: Does the story of Martha and Mary honor women as disciples or confine them?
hard.a:
The critical case is strongest in Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza's essay on Martha and Mary (1986) and in Barbara Reid's Choosing the Better Part? (1996). They argue that the word for Martha's work, diakonia, was by Luke's day a word for leadership in the churches (Acts 6:1-4), that the story pits two women against each other, and that it rewards the silent, listening woman while rebuking the active, speaking one. On this view Luke, writing when women's roles were being restricted, uses Jesus' authority to commend women's quiet receptivity and to discourage their public ministry, and the church's long habit of ranking contemplation above action reinforced the pattern.

Other interpreters read the scene the opposite way. Ben Witherington III (Women in the Ministry of Jesus, 1984) and many commentators argue that Mary is placed in the posture of a disciple at a teacher's feet, a place ordinarily kept for men, and that Jesus defends her right to it against the expectation that she belongs with the serving; the story liberates rather than confines. They note that Luke also names women who travel with Jesus and support the mission from their means (8:1-3), that women are the first witnesses of the resurrection (24:1-10), and that Martha is not condemned for serving but for anxiety. Teresa of Ávila and Meister Eckhart, centuries earlier, refused to let Mary be set against Martha. Readers across traditions, including those who differ on women's ordination, can agree that Jesus welcomes a woman as a learner and that the one thing necessary is the same for every disciple. How the story bears on women's leadership in the church today is a second-order question on which faithful Christians still differ.

observe: What are the seventy-two told to carry, to say, and to do when a town welcomes them, and what when a town rejects them?
What question does the lawyer ask first, what question does he ask second, and what question does Jesus ask him in return?
List every action the Samaritan takes for the wounded man. What does each one cost him?
interpret: Why does Jesus tell the disciples not to rejoice that the spirits submit to them, but that their names are written in heaven?
Why do you think Jesus made the hero of the story a Samaritan, and why might the lawyer have avoided saying the word?
What exactly does Jesus correct in Martha, and what does he defend in Mary?
apply: Who is the person or group you would least like to see as the hero of this parable, and what would it mean to learn mercy from them?
Where are you tempted to pass by on the other side, and what reason do you usually give yourself?
What would it look like this week to sit at Jesus' feet before you serve, and what worries would you need to set down to do it?
